stories.title: India's Textiles Ministry launches Centre of Excellence for Handloom Technology at IIT Delhi to modernize a 3.5-million-weaver industry
stories.what_happened: **Union Textiles Minister Giriraj Singh** inaugurated the **Centre of Excellence for Handloom Technology (CoE-HT)** at **IIT Delhi** today, an initiative built with an investment of roughly **₹12 crore**. The centre will work on **loom modernization and ergonomics** (making looms easier and safer to physically operate), **artificial intelligence**, sustainability, and digital knowledge systems for the handloom sector. Alongside the launch, the ministry rolled out **five specific initiatives**: 'Handloom 4.0,' which gives weavers digital tools to measure loom productivity and sustainability; 'Handloom e-Vidya,' a digital learning platform for weavers; and 'HandloomX,' an incubation and accelerator platform for handloom-related startups, among others. Senior officials including Minister of State **Pabitra Margherita** and Textiles Secretary **Neelam Shami Rao** attended the event.
key_points: Union Textiles Minister **Giriraj Singh** inaugurated the **Centre of Excellence for Handloom Technology (CoE-HT)** at IIT Delhi today.
The centre was set up with an investment of about **₹12 crore (₹11.99 crore)**.
It will focus on **loom modernization, AI, sustainability and digital tools** for India's handloom sector.
**Five new initiatives** launch alongside it, including 'Handloom 4.0' (digital productivity tools) and 'HandloomX' (a startup accelerator).
The goal is to connect **academia, industry, designers and weavers** who have historically worked in isolation from each other.

depth.background: India's handloom sector is one of the largest sources of rural, non-farm employment in the country, sustaining millions of weaver households, many working with techniques passed down for generations on manually operated looms. Despite its cultural and economic importance, the sector has long struggled with **low productivity, poor market access, and outdated equipment** compared to power-loom and mill-made textiles, making it hard for traditional weavers to compete or earn a stable living. The government has periodically launched schemes to modernize the sector, and this new centre — a partnership between the **Ministry of Textiles** and one of India's top engineering institutes — is the latest attempt to bring modern technology and design thinking directly to weavers.

stories.title: Sensex jumps 788 points as falling crude oil prices and RBI rate-decision hopes lift Indian markets
stories.what_happened: Indian equity benchmarks opened sharply higher on **August 3**: the **Sensex gained 788.7 points to 78,883.34**, and the **Nifty50 rose to above 24,550**, up nearly 190 points, as crude oil prices fell on news that the US would not carry out threatened new strikes on Iran. **ITC, IndiGo-parent InterGlobe Aviation, and Bajaj Finance** were among the top Nifty gainers. The move comes just two days before the **RBI's Monetary Policy Committee announces its rate decision on August 5**, where most economists expect the repo rate to be held at **5.25%**. It also comes in the middle of India's **busiest Q1 earnings week**, with over 350 companies — including **Bharti Airtel, ONGC, Power Grid, SBI and Titan** — reporting results this week.
key_points: The **Sensex opened up 788.7 points** at 78,883, and the **Nifty added 189 points** to cross **24,550**.
The rally is driven by a **sharp drop in crude oil prices** after the US held off on new strikes on Iran, easing fears of a Middle East oil-supply shock.
**ITC, InterGlobe Aviation (IndiGo) and Bajaj Finance** led the gainers on the Nifty50.
Markets are also positioning ahead of the **RBI's rate decision on August 5** and a heavy week of **Q1 earnings** from Bharti Airtel, SBI, ONGC and others.
**Foreign investors bought a modest ₹277 crore** of Indian equities on July 31, while domestic investors bought far more, **₹2,260 crore**.

depth.background: India imports over 80% of its oil, so **crude oil prices** move Indian markets almost as directly as domestic news does — a fall in oil prices lowers the country's import bill, eases inflation pressure, and is read by markets as good news for corporate margins and the rupee. The past week has been dominated by Middle East tension: **Trump ordered and then called off new strikes on Iran**, and Iran has reportedly signalled openness to reopening the **Strait of Hormuz**, a critical oil shipping chokepoint. That de-escalation is what's pulling oil prices — and by extension Indian stocks — in a positive direction today.

stories.title: Bihar, Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh count votes in three assembly bypolls, with Prashant Kishor's Jan Suraaj chasing its first big win in Bankipur
stories.what_happened: Vote counting began at **8am on Monday** under tight security for three assembly bypolls: **Bankipur** in Bihar, **Manjalpur** in Gujarat, and **Datia** in Madhya Pradesh. In Bankipur, Jan Suraaj founder **Prashant Kishor** was ahead of BJP candidate **Neeraj Kumar Sinha**, with his lead widening to **6,011 votes** as counting progressed through multiple rounds — the seat has 31 total rounds scheduled before a final result. In Manjalpur, BJP's **Satish Patel** built an **8,373-vote lead** over Congress's Bhikhabhai Rabari after the fourth round, with Patel polling 12,941 votes to Rabari's 4,568. In Datia, BJP's **Ashutosh Tiwari** led a three-cornered contest after the first round, ahead of Congress's Ghanshyam Singh and the Aazad Samaj Party (Kanshi Ram)'s Damodar Yadav 'Mandal'.
key_points: Counting began at **8am today** for bypolls in Bankipur (Bihar), Manjalpur (Gujarat) and Datia (Madhya Pradesh).
In **Bankipur**, Jan Suraaj founder **Prashant Kishor** widened his lead over BJP's Neeraj Kumar Sinha to **6,011 votes**.
In **Manjalpur**, BJP's Satish Patel led Congress by **8,373 votes** after the fourth round of counting.
In **Datia**, BJP's Ashutosh Tiwari led a three-way contest with Congress and the Aazad Samaj Party after round one.
Bankipur is the first real electoral test for Kishor's **Jan Suraaj party**, launched after he built his name as a political strategist.

depth.background: Prashant Kishor is a political strategist who ran high-profile election campaigns for parties including the BJP, Congress and several regional outfits before launching his own party, **Jan Suraaj** ('good governance'), to contest elections in Bihar directly rather than advise others. An assembly bypoll (by-election) is held to fill a seat that falls vacant between general elections, and results are watched closely as an early signal of voter mood. Bankipur is a Patna constituency where Kishor is personally contesting, making this the clearest test yet of whether his years advising other parties translate into votes for his own.

stories.title: IMD issues heavy rain alerts across Delhi, UP, Uttarakhand, Himachal, Punjab and Bihar as monsoon intensifies
stories.what_happened: The **IMD** issued forecasts warning of heavy to very heavy rainfall, thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds across a broad swath of northern India over the coming days. **Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand and Jammu & Kashmir** are forecast to see the heaviest rain, continuing through **August 7**, with isolated spots at risk of very heavy downpours. **Delhi, Haryana and Punjab** are expected to see heavy rain between **August 2 and 4**, while **east Uttar Pradesh** and **Bihar** are under alert into **August 5-6**. The IMD has specifically warned that intense rainfall could trigger **flash floods, waterlogging, and landslides**, and it has advised tourists and pilgrims heading to Himalayan states to check conditions before traveling.
key_points: The **India Meteorological Department (IMD)** has forecast heavy to very heavy rain across northern India over the next several days.
**Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand and Jammu & Kashmir** are expected to get heavy-to-very-heavy rain through **August 7**.
**Delhi, Haryana and Punjab** face heavy rain risk between **August 2 and 4**.
**East Uttar Pradesh** and **Bihar** are under alert for heavy rainfall into **August 5-6**.
Authorities have warned of **flash floods, waterlogging and landslides** in vulnerable and hilly areas.

depth.background: India's economy and daily life run on the **southwest monsoon** — the seasonal rains from June to September that supply most of the country's annual rainfall, water its farms, and refill its reservoirs. But the same monsoon that India depends on for agriculture also regularly turns destructive, especially in the Himalayan foothills where heavy rain triggers landslides, and in low-lying northern plains prone to flash flooding. This alert comes as several parts of India — Assam, Kerala, and Gujarat among them — are already dealing with deadly flood and landslide damage this monsoon season, so northern India's IMD warning adds another front to an already stretched disaster-response season.

stories.title: Trump says US-Iran talks begin Monday to lock in a Hormuz deal — but Tehran denies any imminent session
stories.what_happened: Speaking to reporters aboard Air Force One on Sunday, Trump said the US had decided against delivering "a massive attack" on Iran after Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the UAE and Iran itself asked Washington to hold off, with negotiations now set to begin **Monday afternoon**. Trump said the deal being discussed would include the **"Immediate, Complete, and Total"** reopening of the Strait of Hormuz to shipping, plus an end to Iran's nuclear weapons threat, and that he was setting no deadline for reaching it. However, Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson **Esmail Baghaei** told a press conference Monday that there is **no immediate plan** for negotiations with the US, reiterating that Tehran is currently only engaged in talks with **Oman** regarding the strait. The contradiction leaves it unclear whether the direct US-Iran session Trump described will actually happen today.
key_points: Trump says **US-Iran talks** begin Monday afternoon, with **no deadline** set for a deal.
The proposed deal covers a **'total' reopening of the Strait of Hormuz** and an end to Iran's nuclear program.
Trump says the US held off a **'massive attack'** at the request of Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the UAE and Iran itself.
Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson **Esmail Baghaei** denies any immediate plan for direct talks with the US.
Tehran says it is currently negotiating **only with Oman** over how ships cross the strait.

depth.background: The US and Israel have been at war with Iran for months, a conflict that escalated sharply in late July when Iran began targeting tankers to effectively choke off the **Strait of Hormuz** — the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that roughly a fifth of the world's oil passes through daily. After ordering a new wave of strikes on July 31, Trump abruptly reversed course two days ago, citing an emerging deal brokered with help from Gulf states, but Iran never publicly confirmed the same terms Trump described.

thread.previously: We reported that Trump had paused a planned attack on Iran, saying 'the perimeters of a deal' to reopen the Strait of Hormuz had been reached with mediation from Qatar, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia — though Iran had not publicly confirmed the same terms.
thread.changed: Trump now says direct US-Iran negotiations will begin Monday afternoon to nail down that deal, covering a full Hormuz reopening and an end to Iran's nuclear threat. But Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson says Tehran has no immediate plan for talks with Washington and is only negotiating with Oman over the strait — reviving doubt that a deal is actually close.

stories.title: Wall Street opens August bracing for Friday's jobs report as the biggest week of earnings season begins
stories.what_happened: US equity futures climbed Monday morning as investors kicked off August trading, with contracts tied to the **Dow Jones Industrial Average** up 265 points (0.9%), **S&P 500** futures up 0.55%, and **Nasdaq-100** futures up 0.93%. The day's first economic release is the **July ISM manufacturing index**, a widely watched gauge of US factory activity. **Palantir Technologies** reports earnings after the close today, kicking off a week that also includes **AMD, Eli Lilly and SanDisk**. The week's centerpiece is Friday's **July nonfarm payrolls report**, where economists polled by Dow Jones expect the economy added **87,500 jobs**, up from June's 57,000, while the unemployment rate is forecast to edge up to **4.3%** from 4.2%. So far this earnings season, roughly 300 S&P 500 companies have reported, and **85% have beaten analyst expectations**, according to FactSet.
key_points: US stock futures rose Monday, with Dow futures up **265 points (0.9%)** as August trading opened.
Friday brings the **July jobs report** — economists expect just **87,500 new jobs**, with unemployment ticking up to **4.3%**.
**Palantir** reports today, with **AMD, Eli Lilly and SanDisk** also headlining this week's earnings.
Of the roughly **300 S&P 500 companies** that have already reported, **85% beat expectations**.
Today's **ISM manufacturing index** — a survey of factory activity — is the first data point of the week.

depth.background: Each month, the US government's jobs report (officially the 'Employment Situation Summary') tells investors and the Federal Reserve how healthy the labor market really is — a weak number can mean the economy is slowing, while a too-strong one can worry the Fed about inflation. Coming into August, the second-quarter earnings season has been unusually strong, with the vast majority of large US companies beating Wall Street's profit forecasts. That combination — solid earnings, but a labor market that's expected to keep cooling — is what traders are weighing as the month opens.

stories.title: Oil prices drop as Trump's called-off Iran strike eases the war-risk premium baked into crude
stories.what_happened: Trading opened in Asia on Monday with oil prices falling hard: **WTI crude sank 4.5% to $80.89 a barrel**, and **Brent crude lost 4.4% to $84.10**. The move followed Trump's weekend statement that he had called off a planned strike on Iran, saying Tehran and other Middle Eastern countries had asked the US to hold off because the outline of a deal had been agreed. With the immediate threat of a fresh military escalation reduced, traders unwound some of the extra risk premium they had built into crude prices over the previous two weeks. The pullback marks one of the largest single-day drops in oil this cycle, though prices remain well above where they stood before the crisis began.
key_points: US crude (WTI) fell **4.5%** to **$80.89 a barrel**; global benchmark Brent dropped **4.4%** to **$84.10**.
The drop came after Trump said he called off a planned strike on Iran, citing the outline of a deal.
Prices had surged as much as **24% in July alone** on fears of a wider war shutting the **Strait of Hormuz**.
About **one-fifth of the world's seaborne oil** normally passes through that single waterway.
Traders are betting the immediate escalation risk has passed, not that the underlying conflict is over.

depth.background: Oil prices had been climbing for weeks as the US and Israel traded strikes with Iran and tankers came under attack near the **Strait of Hormuz**, the narrow channel between Iran and Oman that carries a huge share of the world's crude. Every time a strike looked imminent, traders added a 'risk premium' to the price of oil — extra cost to cover the chance that supply gets disrupted, even if it never actually is. That premium pushed Brent up nearly a quarter in July alone, one of its sharpest monthly gains in years.

thread.previously: We reported Trump had called off a planned new wave of US strikes on Iran, saying Tehran and other Middle Eastern countries had asked for a pause while the outline of a deal came together.
thread.changed: That de-escalation is now showing up in hard numbers: oil traders spent the weekend pricing out some of the 'war premium' they had added to crude, and prices fell sharply in Monday trading.

stories.title: India's busiest earnings week of the quarter kicks off, with 350+ companies reporting through August 8
stories.what_happened: More than **350 companies on the BSE** are scheduled to report their April–June quarter (Q1 FY27) results between **August 3 and August 8**, making it one of the busiest stretches of the entire earnings season. Marquee names on the calendar include **State Bank of India, Bharti Airtel, ONGC, Power Grid, Marico, Titan Company, Hero MotoCorp, DLF, and Hindalco Industries**, spanning banking, telecom, energy, consumer goods, autos, and real estate. The results will be scrutinised for signs of whether India's economy — already the subject of debate ahead of this week's RBI rate decision — is growing as fast as recent GDP estimates suggest. Analysts will pay particular attention to bank earnings like SBI's for clues on loan growth and asset quality.
key_points: Over **350 listed Indian companies** report April–June (Q1 FY27) results between **August 3 and 8**.
Big names due this week include **SBI, Bharti Airtel, ONGC, Titan, and Hindalco**.
The week spans banking, telecom, energy, FMCG, pharma, autos and real estate.
Investors watch this window closely to gauge how the broader economy is holding up quarter to quarter.
State Bank of India, the country's largest lender, is among the marquee reports investors will parse for credit demand and bad-loan trends.

depth.background: Every quarter, thousands of Indian companies report their financial results in a compressed window, but the first week of August is traditionally one of the heaviest, catching a huge cross-section of the economy — banks, telecom operators, oil producers, consumer goods makers — all at once. Because India doesn't publish detailed monthly GDP data the way some countries do, these earnings reports are one of the clearest real-time signals investors and economists get on how businesses and consumers are actually doing.

stories.title: Parliament's Monsoon Session resumes today with the Supreme Court judges bill back on the table
stories.what_happened: Parliament's Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha, having been adjourned amid continuing Opposition uproar, resume sitting today, August 3. On the agenda is the **Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026**, which would raise the court's sanctioned strength from 33 to 37 judges — a move meant to help the top court clear its backlog of pending cases faster. The bill formally replaces an ordinance the government had already used to make the same change on an interim basis. Whether it gets a substantive debate, or is rushed through like the births-and-deaths bill was, will be a live test of whether the session's gridlock has eased.
key_points: Both Houses of Parliament were adjourned until **today, August 3**, after days of Opposition disruption.
The Lok Sabha is due to take up the **Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026**.
The bill would raise the Supreme Court's sanctioned strength from **33 to 37 judges**.
It replaces an **earlier ordinance** the government had issued on the same subject.
Opposition protests have centred on a **police crackdown on a student march** over exam-related grievances.

depth.background: India's Monsoon Session of Parliament, running from mid-July to mid-August, has been repeatedly disrupted by Opposition protests over how police handled a student march earlier in the session. That disruption has meant several bills — including one on births-and-deaths registration — passed with little or no debate, which critics say undermines Parliament's basic job of scrutinising legislation. The Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill was introduced by Law Minister **Arjun Ram Meghwal** to formally legislate an increase in judges that had previously been done through a temporary ordinance.

thread.previously: We reported the Lok Sabha had passed a births-and-deaths registration bill without debate as opposition uproar over a police crackdown on a student march paralysed proceedings, with both Houses eventually adjourned until August 3.
thread.changed: Parliament is back in session today, and the Lok Sabha is due to take up the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill — a chance to see whether the same disruption continues or business finally moves forward.

stories.title: Beth Mooney powers Trent Rockets Women past Welsh Fire in Cardiff for a second Hundred win
stories.what_happened: At Cardiff, **Trent Rockets Women** chased down Welsh Fire Women's total of **129 for 3** with 17 balls to spare, winning by 8 wickets. **Beth Mooney** led the chase with a rapid 57 off 35 balls, laying the foundation before **Nat Sciver-Brunt (37 not out off 23 balls)** and **Ash Gardner (10 not out off 9 balls)** finished the job together at the crease. The win was Trent Rockets Women's second of the season, marking a positive turn in form after an inconsistent start to their Hundred campaign.
key_points: Trent Rockets Women beat Welsh Fire Women by **8 wickets** in Cardiff.
**Beth Mooney** top-scored with **57 off 35 balls**, setting up the chase.
Welsh Fire were restricted to **129 for 3** from their 100 balls.
Trent Rockets chased the target down with **17 balls to spare**.
**Nat Sciver-Brunt (37 not out)** and **Ash Gardner (10 not out)** finished the innings together.

depth.background: The Hundred is England's short-format cricket competition, played over 100 balls per side rather than the more familiar 20-over T20 format, and features both men's and women's franchise teams competing in parallel tournaments each summer. Welsh Fire Women had been in strong form this season, making this result a notable upset for Trent Rockets Women, who picked up just their second win of the competition.

stories.title: Israel's Gaza strikes kill 17 in the deadliest day in weeks, even as a US-brokered disarmament plan is supposed to be taking hold
stories.what_happened: Israeli forces carried out strikes across multiple Gaza locations on August 3, killing at least **17 Palestinians** — the deadliest single day in the enclave in several weeks, according to Palestinian health officials. In Deir al-Balah, an air raid killed a married couple, 68-year-old Kamal Abu Muailiq and his 59-year-old wife Huda. In Gaza City's Remal neighbourhood, a drone strike hit a tent sheltering displaced people, killing two, including a child. Separately, four people were killed when a strike hit a vehicle in Gaza City, and a person was directly targeted and killed in the Jabalia refugee camp in the north. **Nickolay Mladenov**, the Board of Peace's Gaza envoy, said the past two days of strikes had killed civilians and destroyed medical supplies people depend on.
key_points: **17 Palestinians killed** across Gaza on August 3 — the highest single-day toll in weeks.
An elderly couple, **Kamal and Huda Abu Muailiq**, died in an air raid on their home in Deir al-Balah.
A child was among two people killed in a **drone strike on a displaced-persons tent** in Gaza City's Remal area.
The strikes come despite Hamas reportedly agreeing to **disarm** under a US-drafted peace framework.
The UN-linked Gaza peace envoy says the strikes have **destroyed medical supplies** civilians depend on.

depth.background: In late July, US President **Donald Trump** announced Hamas had agreed to hand over its weapons as part of a broader plan to end the two-year Gaza war. That plan also calls for Israel to gradually **withdraw from Gaza** and transfer administrative power to a Palestinian authority — terms Israeli politicians and much of the Israeli press have received coolly. Two days ago we reported Israeli strikes had already killed nine people despite the supposed disarmament breakthrough, with a senior Israeli minister flatly denying any deal existed to stop the attacks. The gap between the diplomatic announcement in Washington and the reality on the ground in Gaza has only widened since.

thread.previously: We reported that Israeli strikes had killed nine people in Gaza for a second straight day, with an Israeli minister publicly denying any deal was in place to stop the attacks, even as Hamas had reportedly agreed to disarm under a US-backed plan.
thread.changed: The death toll jumped sharply: at least **17 Palestinians were killed** on August 3, the worst single day in weeks, including a married couple in their 60s and a child, showing the 'no deal to stop attacks' stance from two days ago has held even as the wider disarmament plan is meant to be moving forward.

stories.title: RBI's rate-setting committee begins its 3-day meeting today, with markets betting on a hold at 5.25%
stories.what_happened: The RBI's Monetary Policy Committee began its three-day rate-setting meeting today, August 3, with Governor Sanjay Malhotra due to announce the decision on August 5. A Reuters survey of 72 economists found overwhelming consensus for a hold: 68 expect the repo rate to remain unchanged at **5.25%**, four expect a 25-basis-point hike, and none expect a cut. The committee is weighing elevated crude oil prices — worsened by the ongoing Strait of Hormuz shipping disruptions — and monsoon-driven food-price risk against recent strong growth data, with SBI Research raising its Q1 growth estimate to roughly 7% just a day before the meeting began.
key_points: The RBI's **Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)** meets August 3–5; Governor **Sanjay Malhotra** announces the decision on August 5.
A Reuters poll of 72 economists found **68 expect the repo rate to stay at 5.25%**, only 4 expect a hike, none expect a cut.
The repo rate was last cut by **25 basis points to 5.25%** in December 2025.
The committee is balancing **rising inflation risk** from Gulf oil prices and an uneven monsoon against **strong growth** — SBI Research just raised its Q1 growth estimate to around 7%.
Expect the RBI to keep its policy stance **'neutral'** but strike a more hawkish tone in its commentary.

depth.background: India's central bank, the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)**, sets the country's benchmark interest rate — the **repo rate**, the rate at which it lends to commercial banks — through a six-member Monetary Policy Committee that meets roughly every two months. The RBI's job is to balance keeping inflation in check with supporting economic growth; it cut rates in December 2025 to help growth, and has held steady since. This meeting lands at an unusually complicated moment: the Strait of Hormuz crisis (see our linked story) has kept crude oil prices elevated for months, directly feeding into India's import bill and inflation, while heavy monsoon flooding in Assam, Kerala, and Gujarat adds further uncertainty to food prices and growth.

stories.title: Mumbai Indians publicly deny CSK trade talks over Hardik Pandya, calling reports 'contrary' to fact
stories.what_happened: A Mumbai Indians spokesperson pushed back directly on days of trade speculation, saying: 'Contrary to reports, we are not engaged in conversations regarding player trades; any trade would only be possible once the review is complete.' This contradicts specific reports from earlier this week claiming MI wanted CSK's Shivam Dube and Ayush Mhatre in exchange for handing over Pandya, with CSK reportedly offering Dube, Dewald Brevis, and roughly ₹10 crore in cash as an alternative package. The speculation had been fueled by Pandya's weak IPL 2026 numbers — just 206 runs at an average of 22.89 with no half-centuries, and an economy rate of 11.43 with the ball — alongside Mumbai Indians' failure to make the playoffs.
key_points: A Mumbai Indians spokesperson said: **'we are not engaged in conversations regarding player trades.'**
MI says any trade decision can only happen **after its post-season review is complete**.
Reports had claimed MI wanted **Shivam Dube and Ayush Mhatre** from CSK in exchange for Hardik Pandya.
Pandya's IPL 2026 season was poor: **206 runs at 22.89**, no fifties, and an economy rate of 11.43 with the ball.
Mumbai Indians **missed the IPL 2026 playoffs**, fueling scrutiny of Pandya's captaincy.

depth.background: Hardik Pandya has captained Mumbai Indians since returning to the franchise in 2024, but the team has struggled since, missing the IPL 2026 playoffs entirely — a poor result that has put his captaincy and place in the squad under public scrutiny. Speculation about a trade to Chennai Super Kings (CSK), the franchise he started his career away from, built through late July and into this week, with multiple reports naming specific players CSK might offer in exchange, even though neither franchise had confirmed anything officially.

thread.previously: We reported that Chennai Super Kings had joined the race for Hardik Pandya, with reports saying up to seven IPL franchises now wanted him, and that CSK were reportedly prepared to offer cash plus a player swap.
thread.changed: Mumbai Indians has now **officially denied** being in trade talks with CSK or anyone else, saying its post-season review isn't even finished yet — directly contradicting the specific swap terms (Shivam Dube, Ayush Mhatre, and cash) that had been widely reported.

stories.title: Assam's flood death toll climbs to 82 as Kerala reports 8 deaths in a separate monsoon crisis
stories.what_happened: Assam's flood death toll rose to **82** as monsoon rains and river swelling continued to batter the northeastern state, with more than **6,53,100 people affected across 11 districts**, according to state disaster authorities. Separately, and unrelated geographically, Kerala reported at least **8 deaths** from days of relentless rain, landslides and flash floods, concentrated in the state's high ranges — four of the deaths came from landslides in **Kottayam and Idukki districts** alone. Search operations are ongoing for **6 missing fishermen** (four from Thiruvananthapuram, two from Kollam) swept out into the Arabian Sea, plus two Kannur residents swept away by a river. Kerala has moved over **5,700 people** into relief camps, and the India Meteorological Department (IMD) has issued an **orange alert for 12 districts** warning of continued intense rainfall.
key_points: Assam's flood toll has risen from 80 to **82 dead**, with over **6.53 lakh people affected** across 11 districts.
Kerala separately reports **8 dead** from landslides and flash floods, with **8 more missing**.
Six missing Kerala fishermen were swept out to sea near Thiruvananthapuram and Kollam.
The IMD has issued fresh **rain warnings** for Assam, Kerala, Gujarat and Chhattisgarh as the monsoon intensifies nationwide.
The Centre has pre-deployed **NDRF teams** and is coordinating relief with state governments.

depth.background: India's June-September monsoon is a lifeline for its farm economy but also its biggest recurring disaster risk, with the northeast (Assam) and the southwest coast (Kerala) both especially flood- and landslide-prone due to heavy terrain rainfall. Assam's flood toll had already reached **80** as of yesterday, prompting the government to announce a six-month loan moratorium for affected families. The crisis has since widened rather than eased, now stretching across multiple, unrelated states simultaneously.

thread.previously: Yesterday we reported Assam's flood toll at 80 dead, with the government announcing a six-month loan moratorium for affected families.
thread.changed: The toll has since risen to 82, and a second, separate flood emergency has emerged in Kerala with 8 dead and 8 missing, including 6 fishermen swept out to sea.

stories.title: India closes out its best-ever Commonwealth Games with 39 medals — and takes the baton as 2030 host
stories.what_happened: The Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games concluded on **Sunday, August 2**, with a closing ceremony at the Hydro arena. India ended the Games with **39 medals** — 13 gold, 17 silver and 9 bronze — its best tally at a Commonwealth Games to date, even with a smaller sports program than previous editions. **Boxing** was the standout, delivering a best-ever **10 medals including 7 golds**, headlined by wins from **Preeti Pawar** and **Arundhati Choudhary**. India's **judo** team won its first-ever CWG golds through **Asmita Dey** and **Harsh Singh**, building a four-medal tally in a sport where the country had no prior history of Commonwealth success. At the closing ceremony, Indian performers **Shankar Mahadevan** and **Manushi Chhillar** led a 20-minute cultural showcase before the Commonwealth Games flag was formally handed over to representatives of **Ahmedabad**, confirmed as host of the **2030 Games**.
key_points: India finished the Glasgow 2026 Games with **39 medals**: **13 gold, 17 silver, 9 bronze** — its best-ever tally despite a curtailed sports program.
Boxing delivered India's best-ever CWG haul: **10 medals, including 7 golds**.
India's judo team won its **first-ever CWG judo golds**, taking its tally to four medals in the sport.
At the closing ceremony, India performed a **20-minute cultural showcase** led by Shankar Mahadevan and Manushi Chhillar as the Games flag was formally **handed to Ahmedabad**.
**Ahmedabad will host the 2030 Commonwealth Games** — India's first time hosting since Delhi in 2010.

depth.background: The 2026 Commonwealth Games ran in Glasgow from **July 23 to August 2**, a scaled-down edition of the event after several traditional host cities passed on bidding. India has steadily built up its Commonwealth Games strength in boxing, wrestling and weightlifting over the past two decades, and this edition marked a breakthrough in judo, a sport where India had never previously won gold at the Games. Ahmedabad's selection as 2030 host — confirmed in the run-up to this year's Games — makes it India's first Commonwealth Games since Delhi 2010, a Games remembered as much for infrastructure and corruption controversies as for sport.

stories.title: Rain and Mohammad Abbas's shock axing shape Day 1 as West Indies close on 165/3 in the series-deciding 2nd Test
stories.what_happened: Rain repeatedly disrupted play on Day 1 of the series-deciding second Test between **West Indies and Pakistan** at the Queen's Park Oval — only **9.5 overs** were bowled before an early lunch forced by rain, with West Indies **49/1** at that point. Pakistan's bowling was built around spin rather than pace after the team made the **surprise call to leave out fast bowler Mohammad Abbas**; spinners **Ali Usman and Sajid Khan** bowled a combined **25 overs** and took two of the three wickets to fall. **Shai Hope and Justin Greaves** counterattacked in the last 45 minutes of play, pushing West Indies to **165/3** by the close, with Greaves unbeaten on 52. West Indies, who won the series opener by 90 runs, need only a draw or win here to take the series; Pakistan must win to level it.
key_points: West Indies closed Day 1 on **165/3** at the **Queen's Park Oval, Port of Spain**, with **Shai Hope and Justin Greaves** counterattacking late.
Only **9.5 overs** were possible before an early, rain-forced lunch, with West Indies at **49/1** at the break.
Pakistan's **shock decision to omit pacer Mohammad Abbas** was the pre-match talking point, with spinners **Ali Usman and Sajid Khan** bowling 25 of the day's overs instead.
West Indies arrive **1-0 up** in the two-match series after a **90-run win** in the opener, meaning this Test decides the series.
The pitch is shaping up as **spin-dominant**, a shift from the pace-friendly conditions of the first Test.

depth.background: **Pakistan** came into this tour after already losing the **series opener by 90 runs** at the Brian Lara Cricket Academy, meaning they had to win this second and final Test in **Port of Spain, Trinidad** just to level the series — any other result and **West Indies win the series**. The **Queen's Park Oval** is historically one of the more spin-friendly venues in the Caribbean, which shaped both sides' team selection, most notably Pakistan's decision to leave out a frontline pace bowler.

stories.title: Sri Lanka Women seal a rare series win over Pakistan, snapping a 12-year drought
stories.what_happened: Sri Lanka Women beat Pakistan Women by **6 wickets** in the second T20I at the Rangiri Dambulla International Stadium, chasing down Pakistan's total of **175/5** with balls to spare, to win the two-match series **2-0**. **Harshitha Samarawickrama** finished unbeaten on 37 off 22 balls to see her team home, and was named player of the series after scoring 173 runs across the two matches, including an unbeaten century in the first game. For Pakistan, **Shawaal Zulfiqar** top-scored with a maiden WT20I half-century, but it wasn't enough to prevent the loss. The win ends a **12-year wait** for Sri Lanka to beat Pakistan in a bilateral T20I series.

It's Sri Lanka's first bilateral T20I series win over Pakistan in **12 years**
**Harshitha Samarawickrama** hit an unbeaten 37 to guide the chase and was named player of the series
Pakistan's **Shawaal Zulfiqar** scored a maiden WT20I half-century, but it wasn't enough
Sri Lanka chased down Pakistan's **175/5** with balls to spare

This series, played in **Dambulla**, was a chance for Sri Lanka to end that streak against a Pakistan side searching for form of its own.

stories.title: Sophie Ecclestone rips through MI London's top order as Manchester Super Giants Women keep winless MI London bottom of The Hundred
stories.what_happened: At **The Oval** in London, MI London Women won the toss, chose to bat, and collapsed to just **92 all out**, playing without regular player Danni Wyatt-Hodge. **Sophie Ecclestone**, bowling the opening spell of the innings for the first time this season, struck twice early — dismissing both Alice Davidson-Richards and Hayley Matthews — to leave MI London reeling at 1 for 2, before finishing a tight spell conceding just **7 runs off 20 balls**. Ecclestone was named Player of the Match for her spell.

England spinner **Sophie Ecclestone**, opening the bowling for the first time this season, took out both openers cheaply and was named **Player of the Match**.

Manchester chased the target down comfortably, reaching **95/4**.

MI London have struggled all season and came into this match already at the bottom of the points table, still searching for their first win.

stories.title: Modi launches a 100-week nationwide drive to pledge India's youth against drug abuse
stories.what_happened: Modi launched the campaign at 11 AM on August 2 via video conference, with Union ministers Mansukh Mandaviya and Piyush Goyal among those publicly backing it. The stated goal is to get more than **1 crore youth** to take a formal pledge against substance abuse, organized through MY Bharat volunteers. Unlike a single pledge-and-forget event, the plan runs for **100 weeks**, with recurring Sunday activities — sports, walkathons, meditation sessions, cultural programs, nukkad nataks (street plays), art competitions and community discussion forums — intended to sustain public participation. Goyal described it as laying 'the foundation for a Viksit Bharat,' tying the anti-drug message directly to the government's 2047 developed-nation goal.
key_points: PM Modi launched the **'Nasha Mukt Yuva for Viksit Bharat Sankalp Abhiyan'** (Drug-Free Youth for a Developed India pledge campaign) on **August 2** via video conference.
The campaign aims to unite over **1 crore (10 million) youth** in a pledge against substance abuse, coordinated through **MY Bharat** volunteers nationwide.
It kicks off a **100-week** 'Jan Bhagidari' (people's-participation) drive, not a one-day event.
Weekly Sunday activities — sports, walkathons, meditation, street plays, art contests — are meant to keep the campaign active rather than symbolic.
The push is framed as part of the government's **'Viksit Bharat 2047'** vision — reaching developed-nation status by India's 100th year of independence.

depth.background: India has one of the world's youngest populations, often called its **'demographic dividend'** — the idea that a large working-age youth cohort can drive decades of economic growth. Officials have grown increasingly vocal about drug abuse, including synthetic drugs, as a threat to that advantage, particularly in border and northeastern states. **MY Bharat** is the government's existing youth-volunteer platform, used here as the delivery mechanism for the pledge drive. The launch fits a pattern of large, symbolic national campaigns (similar in style to past sanitation or digital-literacy drives) meant to shift public behavior through sustained, repeated engagement rather than a single announcement.

stories.title: SBI Research raises India's Q1 growth estimate to around 7%, days before the RBI's rate decision
stories.what_happened: SBI Research said in a note that India's economy likely grew around **7%** in the April-June quarter, well above the RBI's 6.6% projection, citing stronger auto sales, power demand, exports and industrial production than expected. The bank also pointed to a turnaround in the monsoon: July brought surplus rainfall that cut the nationwide rainfall deficit to roughly **13%**, with reservoir levels back to normal — good news for farm output and rural spending later in the year. The report comes just before the RBI's Monetary Policy Committee meets from **August 3 to 5**, with most economists still expecting the RBI to hold its key repo rate steady at **5.25%** for a sixth straight meeting, since inflation is expected to stay above 5% for two more quarters.
key_points: SBI Research now expects **~7% GDP growth** for April-June, above the RBI's own forecast
The RBI had cut its own Q1 forecast to **6.6%**, citing the Middle East conflict
**July's surplus monsoon rain** cut the nationwide rainfall deficit to about 13%
Strong **auto sales, power demand, exports and factory output** are driving the upgrade
The RBI's rate-setting panel meets **August 3-5**, with a decision due August 5

depth.background: India's central bank, the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)**, sets interest rates roughly every two months through its **Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)**. Heading into this month's meeting, the RBI had actually lowered its own growth forecast for the April-June quarter — called **Q1 of FY27**, India's fiscal year running April to March — to 6.6%, partly due to uncertainty from the Israel-Iran war and its effect on oil prices. State Bank of India's research arm, one of the most closely watched private forecasters, publishes its own 'pre-policy' estimate ahead of each RBI meeting.

stories.title: Jasprit Bumrah ruled out of India's upcoming Test series in Sri Lanka with a knee injury

The injury is **left knee discomfort** that Bumrah has been managing since the **T20 World Cup** earlier this year.

stories.title: Israeli strikes kill nine in Gaza for a second straight day as a top minister says there's 'no deal' to stop the attacks
stories.what_happened: Israeli forces carried out strikes across Gaza on **Sunday, August 2**, killing at least **nine Palestinians** — the second consecutive day of fatal strikes after seven were killed on Saturday. Israeli Energy Minister **Eli Cohen** said on Sunday that **no deal exists** to stop the attacks, and argued that since Israel already controls about **70% of Gaza**, it should move to take the rest. His comments directly contradict the picture of a de-escalating ceasefire that the Trump administration and the Board of Peace have been describing since Hamas signed its disarmament framework on July 31. Hamas, for its part, has said it will not implement its side of the deal — handing weapons to Palestinian-run storage sites vetted by Israeli intelligence — until Israel fulfils its own commitment to withdraw troops from Gaza. Neither side has publicly declared the ceasefire framework dead, but the gap between the announced deal and events on the ground is widening by the day.
key_points: Israeli strikes killed at least **nine Palestinians** in Gaza on **Sunday**, the second straight day of deadly attacks.
Israeli Energy Minister **Eli Cohen** said publicly there is **no deal to halt the attacks** on Gaza.
Cohen said Israel — which already controls **70% of the Strip** — should take **full control** of the rest.
The strikes come despite Trump's announced **breakthrough** on implementing last year's Gaza ceasefire and Hamas's **disarmament agreement**.
Hamas has said it won't act on the disarmament deal unless Israel first **withdraws its forces** as promised.

depth.background: In late July, Hamas signed a **15-point disarmament framework** — agreeing to hand its weapons into Palestinian-run storage sites — in the biggest step yet toward ending nearly two years of war in Gaza. But Israel never fully signed on, saying the deal doesn't meet its demand for **complete demilitarization**, and Israeli strikes have continued through the two-week window meant to work out how the plan is actually carried out. The US-backed **Board of Peace**, which oversees the plan, published the disarmament mechanics on July 31, but implementation on the ground hasn't matched the diplomacy.

stories.title: A 2.9-magnitude earthquake rattles north Delhi before dawn — the second tremor to hit the capital region in two days
stories.what_happened: A **magnitude-2.9 earthquake** struck Delhi's North district at **4:14am on Sunday**, according to India's National Center for Seismology, with its epicentre at a shallow depth of about **8 kilometres** near latitude 28.72°N, longitude 76.96°E. It was the **second earthquake felt across Delhi-NCR in as many days**. Tremors were described as mild, and because the quake struck in the pre-dawn hours, many residents who were asleep did not notice it at all. No damage or injuries were reported.
key_points: A **magnitude-2.9 earthquake** struck Delhi's North district at **4:14am** on Sunday, per the National Center for Seismology.
The quake's epicentre was at a shallow depth of **8 kilometres**.
It was the **second tremor** felt in the Delhi-NCR region within two days.
**No damage or injuries** were reported; many residents asleep at the time didn't notice it.
Delhi sits in a **moderate-to-high seismic risk zone** due to its proximity to Himalayan fault systems.

depth.background: Delhi and the surrounding National Capital Region (NCR) lie in **Seismic Zone IV** on India's four-tier hazard map — the second-highest risk category — because of their proximity to active Himalayan fault lines where the Indian tectonic plate is slowly pushing under the Eurasian plate. Small tremors like this one are common and rarely cause damage on their own, but seismologists watch clusters of minor quakes in the same area as a possible sign of stress building up along a fault.

stories.title: An 'unknown projectile' hits another tanker off Oman, showing the Strait of Hormuz crisis still isn't over
stories.what_happened: The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency (**UKMTO**) said a tanker was struck by an **unknown projectile** early Saturday about **12.5 nautical miles off Lima, Oman**, with the impact damaging the vessel's **engine room**. No injuries were reported and the ship remained afloat, but it lost some maneuverability. In a separate, nearby incident the same day, another vessel reported a **large explosion close to it**, without direct impact. Both incidents sit inside the same narrow shipping lane that has already absorbed a string of similar strikes in July, including on a Qatari LNG tanker. Neither Iran nor any other party has directly claimed this specific attack, continuing a pattern where Tehran neither confirms nor denies individual strikes while keeping the region on edge. The incident adds to evidence that, despite talk of a **ceasefire framework**, the Strait of Hormuz remains a live conflict zone for merchant shipping.
key_points: A tanker was struck by an **unknown projectile** roughly **12.5 nautical miles off Lima, Oman**, damaging its engine room — no injuries reported.
Britain's maritime watchdog, **UKMTO**, logged **two separate incidents** in the same stretch of water within hours of each other.
This is at least the **fourth distinct tanker-strike incident** near the Strait of Hormuz in barely a week, on top of the near-total shipping shutdown already in place.
Traffic through the strait — a passage that normally carries **~88 ships a day** — has been running at roughly **10 ships a day** since the crisis deepened.
**No group has claimed responsibility**; Iran has not directly claimed this specific strike, continuing its pattern of ambiguity around the attacks.

depth.background: The **Strait of Hormuz** is a narrow chokepoint between Iran and Oman that roughly **one-fifth of the world's oil and a fifth of its liquefied natural gas** pass through — there is no practical detour for most of that volume. Since a **US-Iran war broke out in late February 2026**, Iran has repeatedly threatened and periodically attacked shipping in the strait as leverage, while insisting it isn't fully closing the waterway. Independent trackers like **Kpler** have shown traffic collapsing even when Iran doesn't formally claim a blockade, because insurers and shipowners simply stop sending vessels through a war zone. Multiple tankers — Qatari, Saudi and now this latest one — have already been hit by projectiles in the weeks before this incident.

stories.title: Guyana Amazon Warriors beat San Francisco Unicorns by 6 runs to defend their Global Super League title

stories.title: A 'heat dome' sends Las Vegas to 115°F and Phoenix toward 116°F, spiking wildfire risk across the Western US
stories.what_happened: The National Weather Service issued an Extreme Heat Warning on **August 1 at 5:22pm PDT**, in effect through **August 2 at 8:00pm PDT**, covering the Mojave Desert with forecast highs of **110–120°F**. Las Vegas reached **115°F on Saturday** — about 10°F above normal and its hottest day of 2026 — with Sunday forecast at 114°F, just shy of the all-time daily record of 116°F. Phoenix was forecast to hit **116°F (47°C)**, while El Centro, California, was expected to tie or break its own record at **118°F (48°C)**. Heat advisories were also issued for the Los Angeles Basin, Salt Lake City, and other parts of the Mountain West. Meteorologists described the heat dome as likely to be relatively short-lived, easing after the weekend.
key_points: A **heat dome** — a ridge of high pressure trapping hot air near the ground — settled over the Southwest and Mountain West this weekend.
Las Vegas hit **115°F on Saturday**, its hottest day of 2026, just one degree off the all-time daily record.
Phoenix was forecast to reach **116°F (47°C)**; El Centro, California, to a record **118°F (48°C)**.
The National Weather Service issued **Extreme Heat Warnings** across the Mojave Desert, in effect through Sunday night.
Forecasters warn the extreme heat plus dry vegetation is **raising wildfire ignition risk** across the region.

depth.background: A heat dome forms when a large area of high-pressure air gets trapped over a region and compresses as it sinks, warming the air below and blocking clouds that would otherwise cool things down — it's the mechanism behind most major US summer heat waves. The Western US, especially the desert Southwest, has seen increasingly extreme and longer-lasting heat events in recent summers, which climate scientists link to a warming baseline climate. This weekend's dome stretched from Arizona to Montana, hitting cities from Las Vegas to Salt Lake City.

stories.title: India shakes up its coaching staff for the Sri Lanka Tests, naming a new fielding coach and losing an assistant to the IPL

stories.title: Carlos Sainz says he still hasn't decided his F1 future, as Aston Martin's chase for him heats up
stories.what_happened: Carlos Sainz said in comments reported Sunday that **no decision has been made** about his Formula 1 future, as speculation continues to build around a potential move to Aston Martin. stories.title: 1.4-million-year-old footprints reveal our extinct cousin Paranthropus boisei was nearly human-sized — and may have roamed in male groups
stories.what_happened: An international team of US and Kenyan researchers analyzed a trail of footprints preserved along the ancient shore of Lake Turkana, dated to about **1.4 million years ago**. The prints came from **eight Paranthropus boisei individuals** moving together in one place at one time — a rare snapshot of group behavior that bones alone could never show. By measuring the size and depth of the footprints, the team calculated that these individuals stood as tall as **1.8 meters** and weighed roughly **75 kilograms**, meaning some were considerably larger than previous fossil-bone estimates implied. Nearly all the individuals appear to have been adults, and the researchers found no clear signs of females or children traveling with the group, hinting the group may have been all-male. The findings were published in the **Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)**, a leading peer-reviewed science journal.
key_points: Fossil footprints at Kenya's **Lake Turkana** are **1.4 million years old**.
They belong to **Paranthropus boisei**, an extinct side-branch relative of modern humans, not a direct ancestor.
Individuals stood up to **1.8 meters (about 5'11")** tall and weighed around **75 kilograms** — far bigger than earlier bone-based estimates suggested.
Researchers found tracks from **eight individuals**, apparently traveling together, with **no clear evidence of females or children** in the group.
The find, published in the journal **PNAS**, is reshaping ideas about this species' social behavior.

depth.background: Millions of years ago, several different human-like species coexisted in East Africa, and only one lineage — ours — survived to the present. **Paranthropus boisei** was one of these extinct 'cousins,' known mostly from a handful of skulls and jawbones with massive teeth built for chewing tough plant food, which is why it's nicknamed 'Nutcracker Man.' Because complete skeletons are so rare, scientists have had to guess at how big these creatures actually were, and footprints — a rare kind of fossil that captures a living moment rather than just bones — offer a much more direct measurement. The tracks were preserved in ancient lakeshore mud at **Lake Turkana**, a site that has produced some of the most important human-evolution fossils ever found.

stories.title: Indonesian ferry Mutiara Sentosa 2 catches fire off Madura island, killing at least 5 with 41 still missing
stories.what_happened: The ferry caught fire between roughly **6 and 7am local time on Sunday, August 2**, while traveling from Surabaya in East Java to Makassar in South Sulawesi. It was carrying **271 people** when the blaze broke out; passengers described jumping overboard or being evacuated as smoke and flames spread through the vessel. Indonesian search-and-rescue teams, coast guard vessels, and nearby ships responded, pulling **225 people** to safety so far. At least **5 deaths have been confirmed**, and **41 passengers remain missing**, with the search-and-rescue operation still active as of the latest reports. Officials have not yet determined what started the fire.
key_points: The ferry **Mutiara Sentosa 2** caught fire early Sunday while carrying **271 passengers and crew**.
At least **5 people are confirmed dead** and **41 remain unaccounted for**.
**225 people were rescued**, most jumping into the sea or pulled out by nearby boats.
The vessel was sailing from **Surabaya (Java) to Makassar (Sulawesi)** when the blaze broke out around dawn.
The cause of the fire is **still under investigation** by Indonesian search-and-rescue authorities.

depth.background: Indonesia is an archipelago of over **17,000 islands**, and ferries are a primary way ordinary people travel between them since flights are expensive and there's no bridge network like in many countries. That means these boats are often old, overcrowded, and poorly regulated compared to airlines — and fires or capsizes happen with grim regularity; a similar Indonesian ferry fire killed three people in July 2025. The **Mutiara Sentosa 2** was on a routine overnight route between two of Indonesia's biggest islands, Java and Sulawesi, a journey many Indonesians take for work or to visit family.

stories.title: Death toll in Spain's Ceuta border crisis climbs past 70 as tens of thousands who crossed from Morocco are sent back
stories.what_happened: Spanish authorities say the death toll from the Ceuta crossing attempt has now reached **at least 72**, while local officials cited by Sky News put it as high as **86**; most victims drowned trying to swim around the breakwater fence or were crushed in the crush of bodies trying to climb over it. By July 31, Spain said about **50,000 of the roughly 60,000 who crossed had gone back to Morocco**, either on their own or through coordinated returns. Spain has begun installing a **500-metre barrier extension** into the sea at the breakwater to close the gap that let people swim around the existing fence. The Spanish government has called the immediate crisis 'almost entirely reversed,' but the death toll continues to be revised upward as more bodies are recovered.
key_points: At least **72 people have died** (Spanish officials) — some sources report as high as **86** — after roughly **60,000 people** rushed the Ceuta border fence from Morocco in late July.
Most died **drowning near the Tarajal breakwater** or were **crushed in a stampede** climbing the sea barrier that separates Morocco from the Spanish enclave.
About **50,000 of the crossers have already returned to Morocco**, voluntarily or by force, Spanish officials say.
Spain is now building a **500-metre sea barrier extension** to stop future breakwater crossings.
Ceuta and Melilla are Spain's only **land borders with Africa**, making them Europe's most-tested migration chokepoint.

depth.background: **Ceuta** is a small Spanish city on the North African coast, technically part of the European Union even though it sits on Moroccan soil — which makes its fence one of the few places a migrant can walk (or swim) directly onto EU territory from Africa. Morocco has, at times, loosened its own border patrols during diplomatic disputes with Spain, and large numbers of people have surged the fence before, including a similar mass-crossing in 2021. This time roughly **60,000 people**, mostly young men, attempted to cross in a matter of days in late July 2026, overwhelming Spanish police and rescue services.

stories.title: Hadjar says it's 'a bit sad' that F1's 2026 rules turn classic tracks like Spa into some of the worst on the calendar
stories.what_happened: Red Bull driver **Isack Hadjar** said it is 'a bit sad' that F1's 2026-spec cars have effectively re-ranked the calendar's circuits based on how much energy they let cars recover and redeploy, rather than by the quality of racing itself. He singled out **Spa-Francorchamps**, historically one of the sport's most respected tracks, as now among the worst-suited under the new regulations. By contrast, he praised the recent **Hungarian Grand Prix** as feeling like 'classic racing' because its layout favours the new power units. Hadjar made the comments during the summer break, having built a strong second Red Bull season with **regular top-six finishes**.
key_points: **Isack Hadjar** says F1's **2026 regulations** rank circuits by how much energy drivers can recover, not by how good the racing is.
Under the new rules, **Spa-Francorchamps** — one of F1's most iconic tracks — is now considered **'one of the worst' on the calendar** for that reason.

The comments come from Red Bull's Hadjar, who has impressed with **consistent top-six finishes** in his second Red Bull season.
The remarks add to a growing driver debate about whether F1's 2026 technical rules are reshaping which tracks 'work' well, independent of their racing history.

depth.background: F1's **2026 regulations** introduced a major technical overhaul, including new power units that lean more heavily on **electrical energy recovery and deployment** — meaning how much energy a car can harvest and reuse now shapes lap time more than in previous eras. This changes which circuits produce good racing: tracks with long straights and heavy braking zones (which help energy recovery) tend to suit the new cars, while others don't. **Spa-Francorchamps** in Belgium is one of the sport's most historic and beloved circuits, making its slide down the 'best tracks' rankings under the new rules a sensitive topic among drivers and fans.

stories.title: Hamilton warns Ferrari is 'pushing hard' on upgrades as he chases Antonelli's championship lead
stories.what_happened: Lewis Hamilton won the **Spanish Grand Prix in Barcelona**, his **first race win since joining Ferrari**, and says the team is now 'pushing hard' to deliver a meaningful upgrade package for the second half of the 2026 season. Despite the win, Hamilton remains well off the championship pace: **Kimi Antonelli leads the drivers' standings by 50 points over Hamilton**, and by 59 over Mercedes teammate **George Russell**. The season now pauses for F1's mandatory **summer break**, with racing resuming at the **Dutch Grand Prix on August 21-23**. Hamilton's comments signal Ferrari intends to use the break to close the performance gap rather than accept a season defined by Antonelli's early dominance.
key_points: **Lewis Hamilton** says Ferrari is pushing hard on upgrades for the second half of the season, after his **first win for the team at the Spanish Grand Prix** in Barcelona.
**Kimi Antonelli leads the drivers' championship**, **50 points ahead of Hamilton** and **59 ahead of George Russell**.

depth.background: **Lewis Hamilton** joined Ferrari for the 2025 season after over a decade at Mercedes, in one of F1's biggest-ever driver moves, but his start at the team was rockier than expected — many races without a win. **Kimi Antonelli**, the young driver who replaced Hamilton at Mercedes, has instead emerged as the season's championship frontrunner. stories.title: Adrian Newey is quietly building Aston Martin's future title car — and Carlos Sainz is tipped to drive it

stories.title: Trump says Iran has agreed to a 'total' reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, as Tehran and Oman near a deal on the waterway
stories.what_happened: President Trump said Saturday night that Iran had agreed to a **'total' reopening of the Strait of Hormuz**, after he canceled a planned joint US-Israeli strike on Iranian energy infrastructure in order to let negotiations continue. Secretary of State **Marco Rubio** and Vice President JD Vance are leading the US side of the talks; Rubio said the earlier US strikes had targeted Iranian defense infrastructure and that Iran has agreed to a 'rough framework' for a broader peace deal, which would include easing sanctions and unfreezing Iran's overseas assets in exchange for Iran giving up nuclear weapons. Separately, Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said talks with Oman over a new maritime route through the strait — separate from existing shipping corridors — are in their 'final stages.' However, an Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson pushed back on the framing, saying the Oman understanding does not amount to a full reopening, and that the strait will never return to its pre-war status.
key_points: Trump says Iran agreed to an **'immediate, complete, and total opening'** of the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran's FM **Abbas Araghchi** says talks with Oman on a shipping mechanism are in their 'final stages.'

A wider deal would also **ease sanctions** on Iran and unfreeze its overseas assets, in exchange for no nuclear weapons.
Iran's own foreign ministry says the Oman talks do **not** mean the strait returns to its pre-war status — a real gap between Trump's framing and Tehran's.

depth.background: The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow shipping channel between Iran and Oman through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil and a large share of its liquefied natural gas passes daily — making it one of the most important **chokepoints** in global energy trade. Since a US-Israeli air war against Iran began in February 2026 (following the assassination of Iran's supreme leader), Iran has largely blocked the strait, boarding ships, laying mines, and attacking tankers, sending oil and shipping costs higher worldwide. Trump has repeatedly threatened and then paused further strikes on Iran over recent months while pushing for a deal to reopen the waterway.

stories.title: India ends Commonwealth Games 2026 with 39 medals and a historic boxing haul — its best-ever Games boxing performance
stories.what_happened: India concluded the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games with **39 medals** — 13 gold, 17 silver, and 9 bronze — finishing 4th in the overall standings. Boxing was the standout: Indian boxers won 10 medals including a record **7 golds**, the most golds any country has won in boxing at a single Commonwealth Games, surpassing the previous mark of 6 held by England (at London 1934 and Gold Coast 2018) and matched by Canada at Edinburgh 1986. Gold medals came from Preeti Pawar, Jaismine Lamboria, Arundhati Choudhary, Priya Ghanghas, Sachin Siwach, Ankush Panghal, and Sakshi Chaudhary, with Jadumani Singh, Lovlina Borgohain, and Narender Berwal taking silver. India's para-athletes also had their best-ever Games, winning 7 medals — 3 gold, 2 silver, 2 bronze — matching the country's combined para medal tally from every previous Commonwealth Games put together.
key_points: India finished **4th overall** at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games with **39 medals**: 13 gold, 17 silver, 9 bronze.

depth.background: The Commonwealth Games are a multi-sport event held every four years among athletes from Commonwealth nations — a lower-profile cousin of the Olympics, but still a major stage for Indian athletes, especially in sports like boxing, wrestling, and weightlifting where India traditionally performs well. This year's Glasgow edition, held July 23 to August 2, notably dropped several sports India usually medals heavily in — wrestling, badminton, table tennis, hockey, and shooting — which made a strong overall tally harder to achieve and puts extra weight on India's performance in the sports that remained.

stories.title: Rain washes out Jaffna Kings' LPL clash, eliminating Dambulla Sixers and confirming the four playoff teams

stories.title: Ukraine hits a Russian air base and oil refinery deep inside Russia as strikes on both sides kill at least 14

Hours earlier, Russia had launched its own large barrage — **35 missiles, mostly ballistic, plus nearly 190 drones** — primarily targeting Kyiv and the surrounding region, killing at least **9** and injuring **40**. Combined, the two nights of strikes killed at least **14 people** across both countries. The exchange comes as Russia's ground offensive, running since roughly mid-May, continues to make minimal territorial progress.

Russia claims it shot down **635 drones**, but the strikes still killed at least **9 people** on Russian soil.

stories.title: F1's return to Africa is 'progressing very well,' says F1 boss Domenicali, with South Africa and Rwanda competing to host
stories.what_happened: Speaking about F1's long-running effort to add an African round, CEO **Stefano Domenicali** said negotiations are **'progressing very well,'** while cautioning the process is deliberately not being rushed. F1 says any new African race needs three things confirmed first: investment that benefits the local community beyond race weekend itself, adequate infrastructure (hotels, roads, airports — not just a track), and an economic base able to sustain the event long-term. Two bids are currently in play: **South Africa**, where the government has opened a tender process for a race at either the historic **Kyalami** circuit or a new street circuit around Cape Town's **Green Point** district, and **Rwanda**, which has proposed a circuit on the outskirts of capital **Kigali**. Domenicali indicated a South African race realistically won't happen before **2029**, while separately suggesting Turkey could return to the calendar as soon as **2027**.
key_points: F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali says talks to bring a **Grand Prix back to Africa** are progressing well.
Africa is the only continent F1 currently has **no race on** at all.
**South Africa** (Kyalami or a Cape Town street circuit) and **Rwanda** (Kigali) are both bidding to host.
F1 wants guarantees on **community investment, infrastructure, and long-term economic viability** before committing.
Domenicali suggests a South African race is unlikely before **2029**, while Turkey could return sooner, in 2027.

depth.background: Formula 1 last raced in Africa at the **1993 South African Grand Prix** at Kyalami — over three decades ago. Since then the sport has expanded aggressively into new markets (Miami, Las Vegas, Saudi Arabia, Qatar), while Africa has remained the one continent with no round on the calendar at all, something F1's leadership has repeatedly called out as a gap it wants to close as the sport globalizes.

stories.title: California's AI Transparency Act kicks in today, forcing ChatGPT-scale AI tools to watermark what they generate
stories.what_happened: As of today, any generative-AI provider serving more than **one million monthly users in California** is legally required to embed a **latent (hidden) watermark** in every AI-generated image, video, and audio clip it produces, carrying machine-readable metadata about its origin. Providers must also let users add a **visible on-screen label** flagging content as AI-made, and must publish a **free tool** the public can use to check whether a piece of content was AI-generated. The law's scope was widened last year to also apply to **large online platforms that host AI content** and to **camera/device manufacturers**. Non-compliant companies face financial penalties under California law. The effective date, August 2, 2026, was chosen specifically to coincide with the **EU AI Act's** own deadline for high-risk AI systems, signaling regulators on both sides of the Atlantic are converging on the same rulebook.
key_points: California's **SB 942** becomes legally enforceable today, hitting any generative-AI provider with **over 1 million California users**.
Covered companies must embed a **hidden, machine-readable watermark** in AI-made images, video and audio, plus a visible label users can toggle on.
They must also offer a **free public detection tool** so anyone can check if a file was AI-generated.
The law's effective date was deliberately timed to **line up with the EU AI Act's** own high-risk enforcement date, a coordinated global push.
It followed years of delay: signed in **2024**, then amended in **October 2025** to widen its scope before finally taking effect.

depth.background: Generative AI tools that create photorealistic images, cloned voices and deepfake video have become cheap and widespread, and there has been no reliable, standardized way for an ordinary person to tell if something they're looking at is real. California's legislature passed the **AI Transparency Act (SB 942)** in 2024 to close that gap for the world's biggest AI makers, since California is home to most major AI labs. Regulators expanded the bill in 2025 (via a companion law, AB 853) to also cover **large platforms that host AI content** and even **device manufacturers**, not just the AI companies themselves. The rollout was delayed multiple times as companies lobbied over technical feasibility.

stories.title: F1 has gone dark for two weeks — here's the rule that forces every team to down tools at the same time
stories.what_happened: Every F1 team is currently in the middle of its **mandatory 14-day shutdown**, during which no work related to car performance is allowed to happen at all — that covers design, development, manufacturing of parts, and simulator running, and even extends to banning emails, calls, or meetings about performance topics. Teams must log their activity during the period, and those logs can be requested by the FIA at any time; the governing body also uses factory access-control systems to track who enters and exits team facilities, and can run random checks if it suspects a team is secretly working. The rule is designed to ensure no team gains a development advantage by simply outworking its rivals during the break, and to give F1's notoriously overworked staff two guaranteed weeks off.
key_points: F1's **mandatory summer shutdown** is underway: a **14 consecutive-day** period where all teams must stop performance-related work.
For 2026, the shutdown falls between the **Hungarian Grand Prix** (July 24-26) and the **Dutch Grand Prix** (August 21-23).
Banned activities include **car design, development, part production, and even simulator use** — plus emails or meetings about performance.
The **FIA enforces it** using factory access-control logs and can conduct **random checks** if it suspects a team cheated the rule.
The rule exists to **control costs** and give burned-out team staff a genuine break from F1's relentless calendar.

depth.background: F1 teams work on a punishing schedule — most of the grid runs **24 races a year** plus constant car development in between, which used to mean near year-round work for engineering staff. The FIA introduced the mandatory shutdown period years ago as both a cost-control measure (stopping wealthier teams from just working through the summer to gain an advantage) and a wellbeing measure for overworked staff. stories.title: India's Cabinet approves ₹84,084 crore 'Samudra Manthan' plan to unlock offshore oil and gas
stories.what_happened: The Cabinet, chaired by PM Modi, approved the scheme with an outlay of **₹84,084 crore** for implementation through FY 2030-31. Unlike earlier exploration-only schemes, Samudra Manthan integrates geological surveys, deep-sea drilling, scientific research, production infrastructure, digital monitoring, domestic manufacturing support and workforce skilling under a single framework. The government projects it will catalyse reserve additions of more than **600 million metric tons of oil equivalent (MMTOE)**, substantially increase offshore exploration activity, and generate large-scale employment, while building a globally competitive domestic offshore-technology and services industry.

depth.background: India imports the large majority of the crude oil it consumes, which means global oil-price swings and shipping disruptions hit the economy directly — a vulnerability already on display today with the ongoing Strait of Hormuz shipping crisis. 'Samudra Manthan' takes its name from an ancient Indian legend about churning the ocean to reveal hidden treasures, used here as a metaphor for extracting value from India's offshore waters. Previous Indian offshore exploration efforts have been criticized as underfunded and fragmented across agencies; this scheme is designed to consolidate exploration, production infrastructure and skill-building under one Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas program.

stories.title: Japan's Kumamoto earthquake death toll climbs to 38 as rescue crews keep clearing rubble a week on

stories.title: Kerala landslides kill 8 as rain traps six fishermen at sea and forces 5,700 into relief camps

stories.title: The EU's new AI transparency law kicks in today — chatbots and deepfakes must now say what they are
stories.what_happened: As of today, any company offering a chatbot, AI voice assistant, or AI avatar to EU users must make it unmistakable, at first contact, that the user is talking to software, not a person. Separately, anyone who publishes a **deepfake** — a photo, video or audio clip that's been AI-generated or manipulated to look real — has to disclose that at the point the audience first sees or hears it, in a way that's "clear and distinguishable," not buried in fine print. AI systems that generate synthetic text, image, audio or video content also now have to mark their outputs in a machine-readable format (invisible metadata a platform can detect) wherever that's technically possible. Systems that read people's emotions or sort them into categories using biometric data (face, voice, gait) must tell those people what the system is doing to them. The rules cover professional and commercial use; a person using AI purely for personal, non-commercial reasons is exempt, as is clearly-labelled satire, art and fiction. National regulators in each of the 27 member states are responsible for enforcement, and the European Commission has already published a voluntary **Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content** that companies could sign by July 22 to get a legal safe harbour showing good-faith compliance.
key_points: **Article 50** of the EU AI Act becomes legally enforceable today, **August 2, 2026**, across all **27 EU member states**.
Any chatbot or AI agent must now tell a user **'you're talking to a machine'** the first time they interact.
AI-generated or altered images, audio and video — **deepfakes** — must carry a **clear, visible label** disclosing they're synthetic.
Companies that don't comply face fines up to **€15 million or 3% of global annual turnover**, whichever is bigger.
AI tools already on the market get a grace period to **December 2, 2026** to add invisible, machine-readable watermarks.

depth.background: The **EU AI Act**, passed in 2024, is the world's first broad law regulating artificial intelligence, and it doesn't switch on all at once — it phases in obligations over several years, toughest rules for the riskiest AI first. Most of the Act polices *how AI systems work* (banning certain uses, requiring risk assessments for high-stakes systems like hiring or credit tools); **Article 50 is different — it polices honesty, not safety**. It says people have a right to know when they're dealing with a machine or looking at something a machine made, no matter how safe or harmless that AI system otherwise is. This obligation was written into the law back in 2024 with a fixed countdown clock, and today is simply the day that clock hits zero.

stories.title: Trump calls off planned new strikes on Iran, citing a deal in the works to reopen the Strait of Hormuz

stories.title: Odisha's Cabinet clears a plan to run its biggest cities as single economic zones, starting with Bhubaneswar-Cuttack-Puri-Paradeep
stories.what_happened: Odisha's Cabinet approved amendments to the state's **Odisha Development Authorities (ODA) Act** on Friday, creating a new legal category called an **Economic Region Development Authority (ERDA)** — a single planning and governing body for a cluster of cities and districts that together form one economic region.
